assumptions.subject: workload
assumptions.statement: 2,600 pages/s sustained, about 225 million pages/day. That rate is SET BY the seen-set tier, not chosen: correcting dedupe to IRLbot's measured 61.9 link-checks per page (see the dedupe assumption) drops the drawn 2-node Redis tier from ~20,000 to ~3,230 pages/s, and 2,600 pages/s is what this fleet, exactly as drawn, sustains inside that ceiling. The earlier 3,000 pages/s headline rested on an un-cited '~10 checks per page' and would leave the same seen-set above 90% utilised. Nothing else in the fleet was resized to reach this number, so the correct reading is: to crawl faster, add Redis nodes FIRST — fetchers, parsers and brokers all still have headroom here. NOTE THE UNIT: a crawler is not user-driven, so 'system_rps' here is pages per second moving through the pipeline and each flow is a PIPELINE PATH, not a user journey. Nothing in this design is latency-sensitive to a human.

assumptions.subject: fetch
assumptions.statement: A fetcher is I/O bound, not CPU bound: ~200 pages/s per instance comes from holding hundreds of concurrent connections, not from per-page work. The 250 ms base latency is the REMOTE SITE's response time, which the engine treats as service time — so the fetch row's latency reflects the internet, not your infrastructure, and no amount of local optimisation moves it.

assumptions.subject: q
assumptions.statement: Frontier capacity is stated in PAGES/s, not messages/s. Each crawled page costs ~11 frontier operations (1 dequeue plus ~10 newly discovered URLs enqueued); a broker sustaining ~30,000 msg/s therefore carries ~2,700 pages/s. The ~10 enqueues is the right quantity here and is deliberately conservative: the frontier only ever enqueues URLs that turned out to be NEW, and IRLbot measured 41,502,195,631 unique pages found from 6,380,051,942 crawled = 6.5 new URLs per page. Do NOT confuse this with the dedupe row's 61.9, which counts every link CHECKED. Same convention as that row: the engine does support a >1 visit ratio (visit_prob is expected visits per request, and youtube.json uses 6.0), but this file carries frontier and dedupe fan-out in the capacity input instead, so that every tier's number reads in pages/s — declared here, not hidden.

assumptions.subject: dedupe
assumptions.statement: Dedupe capacity is likewise in PAGES/s, and THIS is the tier that binds this design. Every link extracted from a page must be checked against the seen-set before you know whether it is new. IRLbot (Lee, Leonard, Wang & Loguinov, WWW 2008) parsed 394,619,023,142 links out of 6,380,051,942 unique HTML pages in a 41-day single-server crawl = 61.9 links checked per page (the paper's own analytical model uses l = 59), and names 'the complexity of verifying uniqueness of URLs' as the first performance bottleneck it hit. At 61.9 checks/page a 100,000 ops/s Redis node carries ~1,616 pages/s, not the ~10,000 that an un-cited '~10 checks per page' implied. That was a 6.2x error and it mattered: it parked this tier at ~15% utilisation and sent the reader off to optimise the fetcher fleet, when the seen-set is what a real crawler runs out of first. The 100,000 ops/s per node is NOT a cited measurement — it is a conservative single-node Redis rule of thumb, and it is the weaker half of this row; only the 61.9 checks/page is measured. The set is Bloom-filtered, so it can report a URL as seen when it was not (a false positive silently drops a page); it never re-crawls one it has truly seen.

assumptions.subject: parse
assumptions.statement: Parsing is the CPU floor of a crawler: ~150 pages/s per instance for HTML parse, boilerplate removal, link extraction and canonicalisation. It and the fetch fleet are the two largest line items, and they are the two the engine sizes most confidently.

assumptions.subject: store
assumptions.statement: S3 PUTs are NOT a constraint for a crawler, because pages are batched into WARC files before they are written. Common Crawl's CC-MAIN-2026-34 (August 2026) packs 2.14 billion pages into 100,000 WARC files = ~21,400 pages per object, so the crawl flow charges one PUT per 20,000 pages (visit_prob 0.00005, rounded conservatively against the measured 21,400) and this row sits near 0% of the ~3,500 PUT/s-per-prefix S3 ceiling across 2 hashed prefixes. The previous model charged one PUT per PAGE and showed 41.6%, contradicting its own 'WARC batches' label. What the object store actually costs you is STORAGE: the same crawl publishes 84.78 TiB of compressed WARC for those 2.14 billion pages = 42.5 KB per page, so ~2,522 pages/s stored for 30 days is ~278 TB/month, not the ~778 TB the un-cited '~100 KB/page' implied — the old figure overstated this design's single largest cost line by ~2.3x. Storage, not compute, is still this architecture's dominant cost, and it grows every month rather than plateauing.

assumptions.subject: dns
assumptions.statement: GAP — DNS resolution is NOT modelled as a tier. It is folded into the fetch row's 250 ms. Omitting it is a defensible L0 simplification; omitting it silently is not, because it is the classic way a crawler misses its own fetch numbers. Najork & Heydon (Mercator, Compaq SRC Research Report 173, 26 Sep 2001) record that 'DNS name resolution is a well-documented bottleneck of most web crawlers' and that before they wrote a custom multithreaded resolver, 'performing DNS lookups accounted for 70% of each thread's elapsed time. Using our custom resolver reduced that elapsed time to 14%.' On a stock blocking resolver the fetch row is wrong by roughly that factor and nothing in this model will warn you — size a caching, multithreaded resolver before you trust it.

assumptions.subject: engine
assumptions.statement: Politeness (per-host crawl delay) is the real constraint on a crawler and is a SCHEDULING property the engine cannot express: it caps how fast you may hit one host, independent of how much fetch capacity you own. The engine will happily tell you 19 fetchers are enough while a per-host budget leaves them idle. Treat the fetch sizing as an upper bound on useful capacity.

_library.summary: Politeness-scheduled crawl pipeline: URL frontier, async fetchers, CPU-bound parsers, Bloom dedupe and a raw-page object store.
